properties.decision:
PROPOSED, NOT SETTLED. Submitted by @ajs from flo2 (docs/proposals/multi-graph-hosting.md, written against reflow2 0.24.0) as the concrete architectural answer to the hosting question that req:many-designs-one-service deliberately left open — that requirement's own statement says "this is deliberately silent on where the designs live: one process per design and one holding many are both answers to it, and that is the hosting question, not this requirement." This is that question being answered.

THE ANSWER: one process opens, serves and closes SEVERAL design graphs at once, with each client session attached to exactly one — instead of the process binding one graph directory at startup and holding it for its whole life.

TWO MISREADINGS KILLED EXPLICITLY, because both make the change sound far more dangerous than it is. (1) IT DOES NOT RELAX SINGLE-WRITER. RocksDB's exclusive lock is held PER DIRECTORY; nothing prevents one process holding many directories and many locks. Each design keeps exactly the single-writer guarantee it has today. The proposal is to hold N single-writer stores, not to make one store multi-writer. (2) IT IS NOT MANY DESIGNS INSIDE ONE STORE. graph_id already namespaces every stored key, so co-habiting is technically possible — and it is the wrong answer.

THE ALTERNATIVE CONSIDERED AND REJECTED — many designs inside a single RocksDB store, relying on graph_id namespacing. Rejected because it would collapse the per-project directory the rest of reflow2 is built on: per-project export and the committed design document, backups and --import restore, the sidecar identity/version/sync files, the git merge driver, and the plain fact that a project's design lives under its own .reflow2/. It also makes identity.rs's silent failure mode — a design opened under the wrong id presents as EMPTY — considerably easier to hit. The gain is a smaller number of open RocksDB instances, which is a resource optimisation, not an architectural benefit. NOTE: this is the same shape as dec:idea-many-graphs-one-store, which Anthony raised as a brainstorm on 2026-08-05; this proposal answers it in the negative for the HOSTING case.

WHY THIS IS SMALLER THAN IT SOUNDS — the groundwork is already in place, and this is the part worth reading before estimating. ReflowService.graph is already Arc<RwLock<DesignGraph>> (crates/reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs:74), chosen precisely because several client sessions share one server (req:sessions-share-a-graph) — a registry of graphs is a map of things already shaped to be shared. Seats are already per-session not per-process (service.rs:88-93, req:seat-per-client). Per-session service instances already exist and already carry graph, graph_path and content_path (service.rs:2484-2492), so attaching a session to a CHOSEN graph is a change to where those fields come from, not to their existence. Identity is already out-of-band and per-store (crates/reflow2-core/src/identity.rs), designed to be read BEFORE the design is opened — exactly what a registry must do. HTTP already exists (--http and --serve-shared since v0.14.0). Opening is already a plain function call with no process-global state (DesignGraph::open_rocksdb, crates/reflow2-core/src/graph.rs:113). What binds the process to one graph is the CLI contract and the startup path in main.rs, not the core.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAS TO CHANGE. (1) A graph registry with a lifecycle: a process-level map from graph key to open graph, carrying the metadata that currently rides on the service — graph_path, content_path, identity, and the write_gen counter the loop nudge reads (service.rs:94-99), all becoming per-graph. Opening must be on demand and BOUNDED: a cold open builds the full-text index and takes seconds on a large design (shared.rs allows 30 seconds), so the first request cannot be treated as cheap and concurrent first requests for the same graph must collapse into one open rather than racing. Eviction needs a policy — each open graph costs a RocksDB instance with its own block cache, file handles and tantivy index — so an idle timeout per graph (the existing --idle-timeout is per PROCESS) plus a cap on simultaneously open graphs, with a clear error at the cap rather than silent thrashing. (2) How a session says which graph it wants: today --graph-path, fixed for the process lifetime. SELECTION SHOULD BE BY graph_id, NOT BY PATH — a path is a property of the server's filesystem and leaks it to clients, while graph_id is the durable name the design already answers to; the registry maps id to path. Candidates in order of preference: an HTTP path prefix (/g/<graph_id>/, visible in logs and routable by ordinary proxies), an MCP initialize parameter, or a tool call that attaches the session — the last is the worst, because it makes every session stateful in a way a reconnect silently loses and leaves a window in which a session is connected to nothing. (3) The rendezvous convention: shared.rs publishes a sidecar beside each store saying a server holds this graph and where it is, and the election is arbitrated by whichever spawned process wins the RocksDB lock — a convention that assumes one server per graph. A multi-graph server holds several stores and therefore several rendezvous claims, and should publish into EACH held graph's sidecar so an unrelated local session that opens that directory attaches rather than failing its open. (4) Not breaking the single-graph path: the overwhelmingly common case is one project, one directory, --graph-path, and it must keep working exactly as it does, including --only-if-present and the latent surface (main.rs:772) which is what makes reflow2 installable machine-wide without minting a store in every directory. THE CLEANEST FRAMING: single-graph mode is multi-graph mode with a registry of one, pre-populated at startup and with selection defaulted — NOT a second code path. (5) Commands that open the store directly: --import, --export and --stop-shared open it outside the server and currently instruct the user to stop the server first; with one server holding many graphs, "stop the server" becomes a much more expensive instruction because it evicts every other project, so these should either route through the running server or grow a per-graph release.

RISKS ACCEPTED WITH THIS SHAPE. Isolation regressions are silent and severe — a handler that reaches the wrong graph corrupts a design rather than erroring, which is why it is carried as its own requirement rather than as a note here. Resource exhaustion: N open graphs is N block caches and N tantivy indices, and without a cap a busy server degrades in a way that looks like reflow2 being slow. Failure blast radius grows: today a panic loses one project's session; serving fifty, it loses fifty. And flo2 becomes schedule-coupled to this work — under the per-project-process alternative flo2 could have been built entirely around an unchanged reflow2, and that coupling is being accepted deliberately.
properties.name: ACCEPTED 2026-08-06 (conditional) — a hosted reflow2 holds N single-writer stores in one process, one lock each; the directory stays the unit of a design
properties.rationale:
Raised by @ajs from flo2's side of the seam, 2026-08-05, and it is the first time the hosting question has arrived with a concrete consumer behind it rather than as an architecture preference. WHY IT IS RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN AS A RE-OPENING OF dec:multi-writer-architecture: Anthony authorized re-opening that decision on 2026-08-05 ("yes, re-open it"), and per dec:reopen-supersedes a re-opening mints a NEW decision rather than flipping the accepted node — but that new decision ALREADY EXISTS as dec:central-host, whose own rationale says exactly this and cites the same rule. Minting a third node for the same seam would have been the duplicate HEAL later flags and somebody has to merge. So this records the concrete ANSWER and hangs it under dec:central-host, which holds the question.

WHAT IS GENUINELY NEW HERE, and the reason this is not a rerun of the 2026-07-25 argument: dec:multi-writer-architecture rejected a hosted service on cost against confirmed intent — it contradicts req:persistence ("the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo") and req:invocation ("the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio"). Neither objection is answered by this proposal and both still stand for the LOCAL case. What changed is that flo2 is a hosted web app whose whole premise is that somebody who cannot clone a repository or run a CLI can still take part in designing something — and that premise is already accepted intent here, as req:design-reachable-without-the-repo. The proposal does not ask the local case to move; it asks for a second deployment shape alongside it, which is precisely what rule:no-foreclosure was written to keep reachable ("build nothing today that forecloses growing into a hosted, multi-user, multi-project service"). This is that rule being cashed in.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody rediscovers it: dec:multi-writer-architecture's rejection of a hosted service turned partly on permanent operational burden and on putting the design on a machine the user does not control. A container image and a graph registry do not make either objection false — they make it somebody's job. The proposal is explicit that reflow2 has NO AUTHENTICATION OF ANY KIND today and that authorization is flo2's job at the layer in front; reflow2's obligation is only that a session bound to graph X cannot address graph Y. If that split is not stated and held, this decision quietly converts an accepted "no hosted service" into a hosted service with no security story, which is the drift dec:reopen-supersedes exists to prevent.

WHAT WAS CHECKED AND FOUND SOUND, recorded because it is the natural place to look and it is the wrong place: the export is NOT incomplete. Every node type created during a session appears in export_graph's output, including Question, ChangeEvent and Fragment, and adopt_on_import correctly preserves graph_id so a clone adopts the design's identity rather than minting a new one.
